compare.prompt: Both statements are correct. How are they connected, and which one is more precise?

debate.claim: It is fine to use 3.14 for π in every calculation.
debate.forEvidence: For everyday measuring, 3.14 is close enough and keeps the arithmetic easy.
debate.againstEvidence: π is irrational, so 3.14 is only an approximation. Large or precise work needs more digits.

listening.script: Listen to Priya sort some numbers. The number 0.75 ends, so it is rational. It equals 3 over 4. The number 0.272727 repeats the pair 27 forever, so it is rational too. The square root of 81 is 9, because 9 times 9 is 81. That is rational. The square root of 80 is different. The number 80 is not a perfect square, since 8 squared is 64 and 9 squared is 81. So the square root of 80 is irrational. It is between 8 and 9, and its decimal never ends or repeats.

tasks.q: Which number does Priya call irrational?
tasks.why: 80 is not a perfect square, so its square root is irrational.

tasks.q: Between which two whole numbers is the square root of 80?
tasks.why: 8 squared is 64 and 9 squared is 81, and 80 is between 64 and 81.

story.title: The Square Plots
story.goal: decide which square plots can be marked with exact side lengths
story.intro: Tariq is planning square planting plots in the courtyard. Each plot has a given area, and the club needs a side length for every plot before it buys the border stones.

beats.lead: Tariq writes the side length of the first plot as a square root of its area.
beats.success: The area is a perfect square, so he names a whole number side.
beats.redirect: The side is not a whole number, so Tariq checks which two perfect squares the area sits between.

beats.lead: Tariq estimates the side of a plot whose area is not a perfect square.
beats.success: He brackets the root between two whole numbers and gives a close decimal.
beats.redirect: His estimate is far off, so he squares it and compares the result with the area.

beats.lead: Tariq classifies each side length as rational or irrational for the club notebook.
beats.success: He gives a clear reason for each choice, using perfect squares.
beats.redirect: He confuses a long decimal with an irrational number, so he checks whether the digits repeat.

story.ending: The club marks the plots with careful measurements, and Tariq can explain which side lengths are exact and which are estimates.

panels.says: The decimal 0.333… goes on forever, so it must be irrational.
Does it have a pattern?
Yes. The 3 repeats forever.
A repeating decimal can be written as a fraction. It is one third.
So an irrational decimal has no end and no pattern.

predict.q: Before Jamal sorts the next group, predict which of these numbers is irrational.
predict.why: 0.666… repeats and equals 2/3. √36 equals 6. But 30 is not a perfect square, so √30 is irrational.

transfer.relationship: A square root names the side length of a square whose area is given
phrasings: √50 inches
The side of a square tile whose area is 50 square inches
The positive number that multiplied by itself equals 50
A length between 7 and 8 inches, about 7.07 inches

decoys.why: This is half of 50, not the number that multiplies by itself to give 50.
A side is a length, so its unit is inches. Square inches measure area.

modeling.title: Will the square rug fit?
modeling.scenario: A fictional reading club wants a square rug with an area of 30 square feet. The corner for the rug is 5.5 feet wide. The measurements are invented for this exercise.
assumptions: The rug is an exact square with sides of equal length.
The corner is a straight, empty space with no furniture.
A rug fits if its side is no longer than the width of the corner.
prompts: Use perfect squares to name the two whole numbers the side length is between.
Test 5.4 and 5.5 by squaring them. Decide whether the rug fits.
Is the side length a rational number? Explain.
limits: A real rug has a thickness and a fringe that the model ignores.
A decimal estimate is an approximation, so the true side length is slightly different.

sentence.base: The number √50 is an irrational number.
sentence.because: The number √50 is an irrational number because 50 is not a perfect square, and its decimal never ends or repeats.
sentence.but: The number √49 has a square root sign, but it is rational because 49 is a perfect square.
sentence.so: The number 50 is between 49 and 64, so √50 is between 7 and 8.

diagnostic.prompt: Sort these numbers as rational or irrational: 0.125, √64, √12 and 0.454545… Explain one of your choices in a full sentence.
lookFor: Sorts 0.125, √64 and 0.454545… as rational and √12 as irrational
Uses perfect squares or repeating patterns as the reason
Does not call a number irrational just because it has a root sign or a long decimal
diagnostic.language: Let the student sort the number cards first and point to the reason on each card. If the sort is right, the barrier is the vocabulary, not the idea.

extension.task: Find an irrational number between 5 and 6. Use squares to show that it lies between them.
extension.reasoning: Explain why √30 is between 5 and 6 but is not a whole number.

en.learning: Your child is learning to tell numbers that can be written as fractions, called rational, from numbers like the square root of 2 that cannot.
en.say: A square root asks one question: what number times itself gives this number?
en.activity: Find square objects, such as floor tiles or windows. Say the area and the side length together. Then guess the side for an area that is not a perfect square, like 20 square inches.

es.learning: Su hijo o hija está aprendiendo a distinguir los números que se pueden escribir como fracciones, llamados racionales, de números como la raíz cuadrada de 2, que no se pueden.
es.say: Una raíz cuadrada hace una sola pregunta: ¿qué número multiplicado por sí mismo da este número?
es.ask: ¿Qué número multiplicado por sí mismo es igual a 64?
es.activity: Busquen objetos cuadrados, como baldosas del piso o ventanas. Digan juntos el área y el lado. Luego adivinen el lado para un área que no sea un cuadrado perfecto, como 20 pulgadas cuadradas.

skills.objective: Students describe and perform translations, reflections, rotations and dilations on the coordinate plane, write the coordinates of an image, and tell which properties each transformation preserves.
skills.studentObjective: I can move a figure with a translation, reflection, rotation or dilation and tell what stays the same and what changes.
skills.languageObjective: I will describe how a figure moves using because, but and so with the words translation, reflection, rotation and dilation.
successCriteria: I name a transformation and give its direction, line, center, angle or scale factor.
I find the coordinates of the image after a transformation.
I tell which transformations keep side lengths and angles the same.
I explain in a full sentence why an image is congruent or only similar to the original.
skills.bigIdea: Translations, reflections and rotations move a figure without changing its size or shape, while a dilation changes the size and keeps the shape.

syntax: The figure was ___ across ___, so the image is ___.
The transformation keeps ___ the same but changes ___.
discourse: Describe a sequence of transformations in order
Justify which properties are preserved

domains.listening: Students listen to a sequence of moves and track where the point lands after each one.
domains.speaking: Students tell a partner the direction, distance, line or center of a transformation.
domains.reading: Students read a game design passage and mark each vertex and each image.
domains.writing: Students write a because, but and so sentence that compares two transformations.

vocab.def: A rule that moves or resizes every point of a figure.
vocab.example: Sliding a triangle 3 units right
vocab.nonExample: Drawing a different triangle in a new place
vocab.sentence: A transformation changes the position or size of a figure.
vocab.morphology: trans- means across and form means shape, so transformation is a change of shape or place

vocab.def: A slide that moves every point the same distance in the same direction.
vocab.nonExample: A flip across a line
vocab.sentence: A translation keeps the figure the same size and shape.

vocab.def: A flip of a figure across a line, so that the image is a mirror image.
vocab.example: Reflecting (1, 2) across the x-axis gives (1, −2)
vocab.nonExample: Sliding the figure without turning or flipping it
vocab.sentence: A reflection across the x-axis changes the sign of y.
vocab.everyday: An image in a mirror or a lake, or time spent thinking about something

vocab.def: A turn of a figure by a certain angle around a fixed point.
vocab.example: Turning (1, 2) 90 degrees counterclockwise about the origin to get (−2, 1)
vocab.nonExample: A slide in a straight line
vocab.sentence: A rotation needs a center, an angle and a direction.

vocab.def: A transformation that enlarges or shrinks a figure by a scale factor from a center.
vocab.example: Multiplying each coordinate by 2 to make a figure twice as large
vocab.nonExample: A slide, which does not change the size
vocab.sentence: A dilation with a scale factor of 2 doubles the side lengths.
vocab.everyday: The widening of the pupil of the eye

vocab.def: The new figure that results from a transformation of the original figure.
vocab.example: The triangle with vertices (4, 4), (7, 4) and (4, 6) after a slide
vocab.nonExample: The original triangle before the slide
vocab.sentence: The image is congruent to the original after a reflection.

misconceptions.belief: A reflection across the x-axis changes the sign of the x-coordinate.
misconceptions.why: Students link the name x-axis with the x-coordinate instead of picturing which direction the point flips.
misconceptions.fix: Plot the point and its image. Across the x-axis the point moves straight up or down, so only y changes.

errorCase.story: Selma reflects the point (2, 6) across the x-axis.
steps: A reflection across the x-axis flips the point over the horizontal axis.
So the x-coordinate changes sign: (2, 6) goes to (−2, 6).
errorCase.explain: A flip across the x-axis moves the point straight down, so the y-coordinate changes sign and x stays the same: (2, −6). The point (−2, 6) is the reflection across the y-axis.

misconceptions.belief: To dilate a figure by a scale factor, add the scale factor to each coordinate.
misconceptions.why: Students treat the scale factor as a distance to move instead of a number that multiplies each coordinate.
misconceptions.fix: Compare the distances from the center before and after. A scale factor of 3 makes every distance 3 times as long.

errorCase.story: Dev dilates the point (2, 3) by a scale factor of 3 from the origin.
steps: A dilation with a scale factor of 3 changes the distance from the origin.
Add 3 to each coordinate: (2 + 3, 3 + 3) = (5, 6).
errorCase.explain: A dilation multiplies each coordinate by the scale factor: (3 × 2, 3 × 3) = (6, 9). The new point is 3 times as far from the origin.

misconceptions.belief: A rotation rule like (x, y) → (−y, x) just puts the same numbers back in the same order.
misconceptions.why: Students read the rule as new labels and miss that the coordinates swap places and one changes sign.
misconceptions.fix: Plot the point and turn a piece of paper 90 degrees. Check that the image lands in the quadrant the rule predicts.

errorCase.story: Rosa rotates the point (4, 1) by 90 degrees counterclockwise about the origin.
steps: A 90 degree counterclockwise rotation about the origin takes (x, y) to (−y, x).
Here x is 4 and y is 1, so the image is (−4, 1).
errorCase.explain: In the rule, the new x is −y and the new y is x. That gives (−1, 4). The point turns from the right side of the origin to above it, so (−1, 4) makes sense.

misconceptions.belief: The image of a figure is just a picture of the same figure, so the original and the image are the same thing.
misconceptions.why: The everyday word image means a photo, so students miss that the image is a new figure in a new position.
misconceptions.fix: Label the original as the pre-image and the new figure as the image. Name both with letters, such as ABC and A′B′C′.

reading.title: Moving a Game Triangle
reading.text: Leo designs a game and moves a triangle on a coordinate grid. Its vertices are at (1, 2), (4, 2) and (1, 4). A translation slides every point 3 units right and 2 units up, so the image has vertices at (4, 4), (7, 4) and (4, 6). A reflection across the x-axis flips the triangle, so (1, 2) becomes (1, −2). A rotation of 90 degrees counterclockwise about the origin turns (1, 2) into (−2, 1). These three transformations keep side lengths and angles, so each image is congruent to the original. A dilation with a scale factor of 2 is different. It multiplies each coordinate by 2, so the image is larger but has the same shape.
reading.simple: Leo moves a triangle on a grid. Its vertices are (1, 2), (4, 2) and (1, 4). A translation slides every point 3 units right and 2 units up. The image has vertices (4, 4), (7, 4) and (4, 6). A reflection across the x-axis turns (1, 2) into (1, −2). A rotation of 90 degrees counterclockwise about the origin turns (1, 2) into (−2, 1). These three keep the size and shape, so each image is congruent. A dilation with a scale factor of 2 makes a larger copy.

questions.q: What are the vertices of the image after the translation?
Why is the image of a translation, reflection or rotation congruent to the original?
questions.a: These transformations keep every side length and angle, so only the position or direction changes.

questions.q: Where does the vertex (4, 2) go under the reflection across the x-axis?
questions.a: (4, −2), because only the y-coordinate changes sign.

wdntb.why: The translation, reflection and rotation keep the figure the same size and give a congruent image. A dilation changes the size, so its image is only similar.

noticeWonder.prompt: A triangle has vertices (1, 2), (4, 2) and (1, 4). Its image has vertices (−1, 2), (−4, 2) and (−1, 4). What do you notice about the two triangles? What do you wonder?

asn.claim: A translation changes the size of a figure.
asn.why: A translation moves every point the same distance in the same direction, so every length and angle stays the same.

asn.claim: Two reflections in a row make a translation.
asn.why: Reflecting across two parallel lines gives a translation. Reflecting across two lines that cross gives a rotation.

wyr.q: To describe a transformation, would you rather use words or a coordinate rule such as (x, y) → (x + 3, y + 2)?

compare.a: Ava reflects (3, 5) across the x-axis by changing the sign of y to get (3, −5).
compare.b: Ben reflects (3, 5) across the x-axis by changing the sign of x to get (−3, 5).
compare.prompt: One strategy is flawed. Which one, and what transformation did that student actually do?

debate.claim: Rotations are harder to describe than reflections.
debate.forEvidence: A rotation needs a center, an angle and a direction, while a reflection needs only a line.
debate.againstEvidence: Once you know the rule (x, y) → (−y, x), a 90 degree rotation about the origin is a quick swap of coordinates. A reflection rule depends on picking the right axis.

listening.script: Listen to Zoe describe moves on a grid. She starts with the point 2 comma 3. She reflects it across the y-axis, and the new point is negative 2 comma 3. Then she translates it 4 units right and 1 unit down, so the point is now 2 comma 2. Finally she dilates the point from the origin with a scale factor of 3, which gives 6 comma 6. Zoe says the first two moves keep a figure congruent. The last move changes the size, so the new figure is similar to the first one, but not congruent.

tasks.q: Where is the point after the translation?
tasks.why: Moving (−2, 3) 4 units right and 1 unit down gives (−2 + 4, 3 − 1) = (2, 2).

tasks.q: Which move changes the size of a figure?
tasks.why: A dilation multiplies distances by the scale factor, so it changes the size.

story.title: The Logo Lab
story.goal: build a repeating logo from one small shape
story.intro: Hana is designing a logo for the school club shirts. She starts with one small triangle and uses transformations to build the full pattern, so every move must be described exactly.

beats.lead: Hana slides the first triangle to make the second one in the pattern.
beats.success: She gives the direction and distance, and the vertices of the image match her plan.
beats.redirect: The vertices are off, so Hana compares the movement of each point with the slide she wrote.

beats.lead: Hana flips a triangle across a line to make the mirror side of the logo.
beats.success: She names the line and the coordinates of the image agree with the mirror line.
beats.redirect: The flip lands in the wrong place, so Hana checks which coordinate should change sign.

beats.lead: Hana enlarges the logo for the banner with a dilation.
beats.success: She multiplies each coordinate by the scale factor, and the banner logo has the same shape.
beats.redirect: The banner logo looks stretched, so she checks whether she multiplied both coordinates.

story.ending: The club shirts and the banner show the same logo, and Hana can describe each transformation she used.

panels.says: I reflected (3, 5) across the x-axis and got (−3, 5).
Where is the point compared with the x-axis?
It is 5 units above it.
A reflection puts the image the same distance on the other side.
So x stays the same and y changes sign.

predict.q: Before Tomas fixes his answer, predict the reflection of (3, 5) across the x-axis.
predict.why: The point is 5 units above the x-axis, so its image is 5 units below it: (3, −5).

transfer.relationship: Every point moves 3 units to the right and 2 units up
phrasings: Slide the figure 3 units right and 2 units up.
The point (1, 2) goes to (4, 4) and the point (4, 2) goes to (7, 4).
Add the arrow 3 right and 2 up to every vertex.

decoys.why: The horizontal and vertical moves are swapped, so the figure moves 2 right and 3 up.
This multiplies the coordinates, which stretches the figure instead of sliding it.

modeling.title: Planning a tile border
modeling.scenario: A fictional art club builds a tile border from one small triangle. The triangle has vertices (0, 0), (2, 0) and (0, 3), with each grid unit equal to 1 inch. The numbers are invented for this exercise.
assumptions: Each grid unit is 1 inch and the tiles lie flat with no gaps.
Every new tile is a transformation image of the first tile.
The tiles are cut exactly to the coordinates.
prompts: Write the vertices of the next tile after a translation of 3 units to the right.
Write the vertices of the mirror tile after a reflection across the y-axis.
A banner tile is a dilation by a scale factor of 2 from the origin. Write its vertices and compare its area with the original.
limits: Real tiles have grout lines and small cutting errors that the model leaves out.
The coordinates describe the shape, but not the color or the pattern the club wants.

sentence.base: A translation moves every point of a figure the same distance in the same direction.
sentence.because: The image is congruent to the original because a translation keeps every side length and every angle.
sentence.but: A translation changes the position of a figure, but it does not change its size or shape.
sentence.so: A dilation with a scale factor of 2 doubles each coordinate, so the image is larger but similar.

diagnostic.prompt: Triangle ABC has vertices A(1, 2), B(4, 2) and C(1, 4). Reflect it across the y-axis and write the new vertices. Then say what stays the same.
lookFor: Changes only the sign of the x-coordinate
Says side lengths and angles stay the same
diagnostic.language: Let the student plot the points and draw the mirror line before writing. If the picture is correct, the barrier is the vocabulary or the sentence, not the transformation.

extension.task: Describe a sequence of two transformations that moves the triangle with vertices (1, 2), (4, 2) and (1, 4) to the triangle with vertices (−1, −2), (−4, −2) and (−1, −4).
extension.reasoning: Explain why the final triangle is congruent to the first one.

en.learning: Your child is learning to slide, flip, turn and resize shapes on a coordinate grid and to tell which changes keep a shape the same size.
en.say: Sliding, flipping and turning keep a shape the same size. Resizing makes it larger or smaller but keeps its shape.
en.ask: If a point at 2 comma 3 slides 4 units to the right, where does it land?
en.activity: Draw a simple shape on graph paper. Slide, flip or turn it and draw the new shape. Say together what changed and what stayed the same.

es.learning: Su hijo o hija está aprendiendo a deslizar, voltear, girar y cambiar el tamaño de figuras en una cuadrícula de coordenadas, y a decir qué cambios mantienen la figura del mismo tamaño.
es.say: Deslizar, voltear y girar mantienen el tamaño de la figura. Cambiar el tamaño la hace más grande o más pequeña, pero conserva su forma.
es.ask: Si un punto en 2, 3 se desliza 4 unidades hacia la derecha, ¿dónde cae?
es.activity: Dibujen una figura sencilla en papel cuadriculado. Deslícenla, voltéenla o gírenla y dibujen la figura nueva. Digan juntos qué cambió y qué se quedó igual.

skills.objective: Students use rigid motions and dilations to define congruent and similar figures, use proportional sides and equal angles to decide similarity, and apply angle relationships in triangles and with parallel lines cut by a transversal.
skills.studentObjective: I can tell whether two figures are congruent or similar and use angle facts and scale factors to find missing measures.
skills.languageObjective: I will explain how two figures are related using because, but and so with the words congruent, similar and corresponding.
successCriteria: I name corresponding sides and angles of two figures.
I decide whether two triangles are similar by checking angles or the ratios of sides.
I find a missing angle using the angle sum of a triangle or angles made by a transversal.
I explain in a full sentence why two figures are congruent or only similar.
skills.bigIdea: Congruent figures match exactly, and similar figures match in shape with every length multiplied by the same scale factor.

syntax: The triangles are similar because the corresponding angles are ___.
Each side was multiplied by ___, so ___.
discourse: Compare congruent and similar figures
Justify a similarity claim with angles or ratios

domains.listening: Students listen to a shadow problem and decide why two triangles are similar.
domains.speaking: Students tell a partner which sides correspond and how they know.
domains.reading: Students read a flag design passage and mark each pair of corresponding sides.
domains.writing: Students write a because, but and so sentence that compares congruent and similar figures.

vocab.def: Having exactly the same size and shape, so one fits on the other.
vocab.example: Two flags that both have sides of 3, 4 and 5 inches
vocab.nonExample: A small flag and its enlarged banner copy
vocab.sentence: Congruent triangles have equal corresponding sides and angles.
vocab.morphology: con- means together and gruere means to agree

vocab.def: Having the same shape, with equal angles and sides in the same ratio.
vocab.example: Triangles with sides 3, 4, 5 and 9, 12, 15
vocab.nonExample: Triangles with sides 3, 4, 5 and 6, 7, 8
vocab.sentence: The banner flag is similar to the small flag.
vocab.everyday: Alike in some way, but not exactly the same

vocab.def: Matching in position, such as sides or angles in the same place in two figures.
vocab.example: The shortest side of one triangle and the shortest side of the other
vocab.nonExample: The shortest side of one triangle and the longest side of the other
vocab.sentence: Corresponding angles of similar triangles are equal.
vocab.morphology: co- means together and respond means to answer, so corresponding parts answer each other

vocab.def: The number that every length of one figure is multiplied by to get the other.
vocab.example: 3, from sides of 4 inches to sides of 12 inches
vocab.nonExample: 8, the difference between 4 and 12
vocab.sentence: The scale factor from the small flag to the banner is 3.

vocab.def: A line that crosses two or more other lines.
vocab.example: A road that crosses two parallel train tracks
vocab.nonExample: A road that runs along one of the train tracks
vocab.sentence: A transversal crossing parallel lines makes equal alternate interior angles.

vocab.def: An angle outside a polygon, formed by one side and the extension of the next side.
vocab.example: A 110 degree angle outside a triangle with inside angles of 50, 60 and 70 degrees
vocab.nonExample: The 70 degree angle inside the triangle
vocab.sentence: An exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the two remote interior angles.

misconceptions.belief: To make a similar triangle, add the same number to every side.
misconceptions.why: Adding the same amount keeps the differences between sides, which students confuse with keeping the shape.
misconceptions.fix: Test with ratios. Compare each new side with its matching old side by division, and see whether the results agree.

errorCase.story: Dara makes a larger triangle from one with sides 2, 5 and 6.
steps: The first triangle has sides 2, 5 and 6.
To make a similar triangle, add 4 to each side to get 6, 9 and 10.
So the new triangle is similar to the first.
errorCase.explain: Similar triangles multiply every side by the same scale factor. The ratios 6 ÷ 2 = 3, 9 ÷ 5 = 1.8 and 10 ÷ 6 are not equal, so the triangles are not similar. Multiplying by 3 gives 6, 15 and 18.

misconceptions.belief: Corresponding sides are the ones listed in the same order.
misconceptions.why: Students pair numbers as they appear in the text instead of by size or by the angles they sit opposite.
misconceptions.fix: Sort both lists from shortest to longest, or match the sides opposite equal angles, before dividing.

errorCase.story: Noor checks whether a triangle with sides 4, 6 and 8 is similar to one with sides listed as 6, 4.5 and 3.
steps: The first triangle has sides 4, 6 and 8. The second is listed as 6, 4.5 and 3.
Pair them in the order listed: 4 with 6, 6 with 4.5 and 8 with 3.
The ratios are 1.5, 0.75 and 0.375, which differ, so the triangles are not similar.
errorCase.explain: Pair the shortest with the shortest: 4 with 3, 6 with 4.5 and 8 with 6. Every ratio is 0.75, so the triangles are similar.

misconceptions.belief: An exterior angle of a triangle is equal to the interior angle next to it.
misconceptions.why: Students see the two angles as a pair and match them, but together they form a straight line.
misconceptions.fix: Draw the straight line. The exterior and the adjacent interior angle add to 180 degrees.

errorCase.story: Pablo studies a triangle with two angles of 50 and 60 degrees.
steps: Two angles of the triangle are 50 degrees and 60 degrees.
The third angle is 180 − 50 − 60 = 70 degrees.
The exterior angle next to the 70 degree angle is also 70 degrees.
errorCase.explain: The exterior angle and the 70 degree angle form a straight line, so the exterior angle is 180 − 70 = 110 degrees. It also equals the sum of the other two angles, 50 + 60 = 110.

misconceptions.belief: Similar means looks about the same, so similar figures can have different angle measures.
misconceptions.why: In everyday speech, similar means a little bit alike, but in geometry it has an exact meaning.
misconceptions.fix: Compare the two meanings in a chart. In math, similar needs equal corresponding angles and sides in the same ratio.

reading.title: Flags for the Robotics Team
reading.text: Rosa designs a triangular flag for her robotics team. The small flag has sides of 3, 4 and 5 inches. For the hallway banner, she makes a larger flag with sides of 9, 12 and 15 inches. Each side is multiplied by the scale factor 3, and the corresponding angles stay equal, so the two flags are similar. Rosa also cuts a second small flag with the same sides as the first. Because every pair of corresponding sides and angles matches, the two small flags are congruent. A congruent figure fits exactly on the original, but a similar figure only keeps the same shape. The angles of both sizes are about 37, 53 and 90 degrees, and they add to 180 degrees.
reading.simple: Rosa designs a triangle flag. The small flag has sides of 3, 4 and 5 inches. The banner flag has sides of 9, 12 and 15 inches. Each side is multiplied by the scale factor 3, so the two flags are similar. A second small flag has the same sides as the first, so those two flags are congruent. The angles are about 37, 53 and 90 degrees, and they add to 180 degrees.

questions.q: What is the scale factor from the small flag to the banner flag?
Why are the two small flags congruent, but the small flag and the banner flag only similar?
questions.a: The two small flags match in every side and angle. The banner has equal angles but every side is 3 times as long.

questions.q: Show that the sides 3, 4, 5 and 9, 12, 15 are in the same ratio.

wdntb.why: The first three triangles are similar to each other, since each is the 3, 4, 5 triangle multiplied by 1, 2 or 3. The triangle with sides 5, 6 and 7 is not similar to them.

noticeWonder.prompt: One triangle has angles of 40, 60 and 80 degrees. A much bigger triangle has the same three angles. What do you notice? What do you wonder about their sides?

asn.claim: Congruent figures are always similar.
asn.why: Congruent figures match in every angle and length, so the scale factor is 1 and the ratios of sides are all equal.

asn.claim: Two triangles with the same perimeter are congruent.
asn.why: A 3, 4, 5 triangle and a 2, 5, 5 triangle both have a perimeter of 12, but their sides are different, so they are not congruent.

wyr.q: To show two triangles are similar, would you rather compare their angles or compare the ratios of their sides?
wyr.b: Compare the ratios of their sides

compare.a: Kai says the triangles with sides 3, 4, 5 and 6, 8, 10 are similar because each side doubles.
compare.b: Lin says the same triangles are similar because the new sides are 3, 4 and 5 more than the old sides.
compare.prompt: One reason is flawed. Which one, and what does the other student check that makes the claim true?

debate.claim: Checking angles is a faster way to prove triangles similar than checking sides.
debate.forEvidence: Two pairs of equal angles are enough, because the third angles must match, but sides need three ratios.
debate.againstEvidence: Angles are hard to measure exactly on a drawing, while side lengths are easy to measure with a ruler.

listening.script: Listen to Omar solve a shadow problem. A tree casts a shadow 8 feet long. At the same time, a 3 foot post casts a shadow 2 feet long. The sun makes the same angle with the ground for both, so the two triangles have equal angles and are similar. The scale factor from the post's shadow to the tree's shadow is 8 divided by 2, which is 4. So the tree is 4 times as tall as the post, which makes it 12 feet tall. Omar checks the ratios of height to shadow. Three over 2 and 12 over 8 are both one and a half.

tasks.q: How tall is the tree?
tasks.why: The scale factor is 4, so the tree is 4 × 3 = 12 feet tall.

tasks.q: Why are the two triangles similar?
options: The sun makes the same angle with the ground for both.
The tree and the post have the same height.
Both shadows are the same length.
tasks.why: Equal angles at the ground and a right angle at the base make the triangles similar.

story.title: The Shadow Survey
story.goal: find the height of the flagpole without climbing it
story.intro: Jamal wants to know how tall the school flagpole is, but nobody can climb it safely. He decides to use shadows and similar triangles, with a tape measure and a meter stick.

beats.lead: Jamal measures the shadow of the meter stick and the shadow of the flagpole at the same time.
beats.success: The two triangles have equal angles, so Jamal can set up matching ratios.
beats.redirect: The two shadows were measured at different times, so Jamal repeats the measurements together.

beats.lead: Jamal pairs the corresponding sides of the small triangle and the big triangle.
beats.success: Each pair has the same ratio, so he finds the scale factor.
beats.redirect: The ratios do not agree, so he checks that he paired the matching sides.

beats.lead: Jamal multiplies the stick's height by the scale factor to find the flagpole's height.
beats.success: The height is reasonable, and he explains the ratio to the class.
beats.redirect: The height seems too small, so he checks whether he multiplied instead of adding.

story.ending: Jamal reports the flagpole's height and shows how similar triangles let him measure what he could not reach.

panels.says: Triangle ABC has sides 3, 4 and 5. I added 3 to each side to get 6, 7 and 8.
Is 6 divided by 3 the same as 7 divided by 4?
No. The first is 2 and the second is 1.75.
Similar triangles multiply every side by the same number.
Then I should multiply 3, 4 and 5 by 2.

predict.q: Before Eli tries again, predict which triangle is similar to the one with sides 3, 4 and 5.
predict.why: Multiplying 3, 4 and 5 by 2 gives 6, 8 and 10, so the ratios are all 2.

transfer.relationship: Every side of one figure is the same multiple of the matching side of the other, and the angles are equal
phrasings: Triangles with sides 3, 4, 5 and 9, 12, 15
The second triangle is a dilation of the first with scale factor 3.
Each side of the larger triangle is 3 times the matching side of the smaller one.

decoys.why: The new sides are 3 more than the old sides, and the ratios 2, 1.75 and 1.6 are not equal.
The ratios are 3, 3 and about 3.2, so the last side does not match the scale factor.

modeling.title: Measuring a flagpole by its shadow
modeling.scenario: A fictional school club wants to know the height of a flagpole. At the same moment, a 5 foot student casts a 4 foot shadow and the flagpole casts a 24 foot shadow. The measurements are invented for this exercise.
assumptions: The sun's rays are parallel, so the student and the flagpole make similar triangles.
The ground is flat and both the student and the flagpole stand straight up.
Both shadows were measured at the same moment.
prompts: Draw both triangles and label the corresponding sides.
Find the scale factor from the student's shadow to the flagpole's shadow and use it to find the height of the flagpole.
If the flagpole's shadow were measured 1 foot too short, how would the height change?
limits: Shadows have fuzzy edges, so the lengths are only approximate.
If the ground slopes, the triangles are no longer similar and the answer is not reliable.

sentence.because: The two flags are similar because each side of the larger flag is 3 times the matching side of the smaller flag.
sentence.but: The small flag and the banner flag have different sizes, but they are similar because their corresponding angles are equal.
sentence.so: Each side is multiplied by the scale factor 3, so the two flags are similar but not congruent.

diagnostic.prompt: Triangle ABC has sides 4, 6 and 8. Triangle DEF has sides 6, 9 and 12. Are they similar? Show how you know and give the scale factor.
lookFor: Pairs shortest with shortest and longest with longest
Finds the ratios 6 ÷ 4, 9 ÷ 6 and 12 ÷ 8 are all 1.5
States the scale factor and concludes the triangles are similar
diagnostic.language: Let the student sketch the triangles and mark the matching sides with colors before explaining. If the matching is correct, the barrier is explaining in words, not finding the ratios.

extension.task: Two angles of a triangle measure 48 degrees and 67 degrees. Find the third angle. Then sketch a triangle that is similar to it but not congruent.
extension.reasoning: Explain why any two triangles with angles of 48, 67 and 65 degrees must be similar, even if their sides are different lengths.

en.learning: Your child is learning that similar shapes have the same shape but can be different sizes, while congruent shapes are exactly the same size and shape.
en.say: Think of a photo and its enlargement. It is the same picture in a different size.
en.ask: A picture is 4 inches wide and 6 inches tall. If it is enlarged to 8 inches wide, how tall will it be?
en.activity: Find a photo and its bigger copy, or a map. Measure two matching lengths on each and see whether they grow by the same number of times.

es.learning: Su hijo o hija está aprendiendo que las figuras semejantes tienen la misma forma pero pueden tener tamaños distintos, mientras que las figuras congruentes tienen exactamente el mismo tamaño y la misma forma.
es.say: Piensen en una foto y su ampliación. Es la misma imagen en otro tamaño.
es.ask: Una foto mide 4 pulgadas de ancho y 6 de alto. Si se amplía a 8 pulgadas de ancho, ¿cuánto medirá de alto?
es.activity: Busquen una foto y su copia más grande, o un mapa. Midan dos longitudes que se correspondan en cada uno y vean si crecen la misma cantidad de veces.

skills.objective: Students use the Pythagorean theorem and its converse to find unknown side lengths, decide whether a triangle is a right triangle, and find distances between points on the coordinate plane and in real situations.
skills.studentObjective: I can use the Pythagorean theorem to find a missing side and to decide whether a triangle has a right angle.
skills.languageObjective: I will explain how I found a missing side using because, but and so with the words hypotenuse, leg and converse.
successCriteria: I name the legs and the hypotenuse of a right triangle.
I find a missing side with a² + b² = c² and a square root.
I decide whether three side lengths make a right triangle.
I find the distance between two points by drawing a right triangle.
skills.bigIdea: In a right triangle, the area of the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the areas of the squares on the legs.

syntax: The hypotenuse is the side opposite ___.
The triangle is a right triangle because ___ plus ___ equals ___.
discourse: Explain each step of a missing side calculation
Justify why a triangle is or is not a right triangle

domains.listening: Students listen to a distance problem and track which numbers are the legs and which is the hypotenuse.
domains.speaking: Students tell a partner how they know which side is the hypotenuse.
domains.reading: Students read a field passage and mark the legs, the diagonal and each squared number.
domains.writing: Students write a because, but and so sentence that explains a missing side.

vocab.def: The longest side of a right triangle, opposite the right angle.
vocab.example: The 10 in a triangle with sides 6, 8 and 10
vocab.nonExample: The side 6, which is a leg
vocab.sentence: The hypotenuse is always longer than either leg.
vocab.morphology: from Greek hypo, meaning under, and teinein, meaning to stretch

vocab.def: One of the two shorter sides of a right triangle that meet at the right angle.
vocab.example: The sides of length 6 and 8 in a 6, 8, 10 triangle
vocab.nonExample: The side opposite the right angle
vocab.sentence: Each leg of the triangle is shorter than the hypotenuse.
vocab.everyday: The part of the body used for walking, or one support of a table

vocab.def: In a right triangle, the squares of the legs add up to the square of the hypotenuse.
vocab.nonExample: 6 + 8 = 10, which adds the lengths instead of the squares
vocab.sentence: The Pythagorean theorem needs a right triangle.

vocab.def: The statement you get by swapping the if part and the then part of a statement.
vocab.example: If a² + b² = c², then the triangle has a right angle
vocab.nonExample: If a triangle has a right angle, then a² + b² = c², which is the original statement
vocab.sentence: The converse of the theorem tells us a corner is square.
vocab.everyday: To have a conversation, or the opposite of something

vocab.def: Three whole numbers a, b and c that make a² + b² = c².
vocab.sentence: The numbers 3, 4 and 5 are a Pythagorean triple.

misconceptions.belief: After adding the squares of the legs, the sum is the length of the hypotenuse.
misconceptions.why: Students stop at the last number they computed, so they report c² instead of c.
misconceptions.fix: Write c² on the answer line and ask what number times itself gives it. Then compare the answer with the legs for reasonableness.

errorCase.story: Pablo finds the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs of 9 and 12.
steps: Use the theorem: 9² + 12² = c².
So the hypotenuse is 225.
errorCase.explain: The sum 225 is c², not c. The hypotenuse is the square root of 225, which is 15. A side of 225 is far longer than the legs added, 9 + 12 = 21.

misconceptions.belief: In a² + b² = c², the two numbers you are given always go in the a and b places.
misconceptions.why: Students treat the formula as a recipe with fixed slots instead of matching c to the side opposite the right angle.
misconceptions.fix: Mark the right angle first. The side across from it is c, whatever its letter or position in the picture.

errorCase.story: Ines knows a right triangle has a hypotenuse of 13 and one leg of 5, and she finds the other leg x.
steps: The sides are 5, 13 and x.
Put the numbers in as the legs: x² = 5² + 13² = 25 + 169 = 194.
So x is the square root of 194, about 13.9.
errorCase.explain: The side 13 is the hypotenuse, so it is c. Then 5² + x² = 13², x² = 169 − 25 = 144 and x = 12. A leg cannot be longer than the hypotenuse.

misconceptions.belief: If a² + b² is close to c², the triangle is a right triangle.
misconceptions.why: Students round their thinking, and the idea of an exact test is new.
misconceptions.fix: Say what the converse requires: the two sides must be exactly equal. If the sum is less than c², the angle is larger than a right angle.

errorCase.story: Omar tests a triangle with sides 5, 6 and 8.
steps: The longest side is 8, so c = 8.
The numbers are close, so it is a right triangle.
errorCase.explain: A right triangle needs 5² + 6² to equal 8² exactly. Since 61 is not 64, the triangle is not a right triangle. Because 61 is less than 64, its largest angle is greater than 90 degrees.

misconceptions.belief: The hypotenuse is always the slanted side of the triangle.
misconceptions.why: Textbook pictures usually show the hypotenuse slanted, so students link the word with the tilt instead of with the right angle.
misconceptions.fix: Find the right angle mark first. Turn the triangle so a different side is on the bottom and name the hypotenuse again.

reading.title: The Diagonal on the Field
reading.text: Lucia sets up a practice field for her soccer team. The field is a rectangle 30 meters wide and 40 meters long. She wants the length of the diagonal path from one corner to the opposite corner. The diagonal is the hypotenuse of a right triangle, and the two sides of the field are the legs. By the Pythagorean theorem, 30² + 40² = 900 + 1,600 = 2,500, so the diagonal is the square root of 2,500, which is 50 meters. Lucia also checks that a corner is square. She marks 3 meters along one side and 4 meters along the other. If the marks are 5 meters apart, then by the converse of the theorem the corner is a right angle.
reading.simple: Lucia sets up a soccer field that is 30 meters wide and 40 meters long. She wants the length of the diagonal. The diagonal is the hypotenuse of a right triangle, and the sides of the field are the legs. The Pythagorean theorem gives 30² + 40² = 900 + 1,600 = 2,500. The diagonal is the square root of 2,500, which is 50 meters. To check a corner, she marks 3 meters and 4 meters. If the marks are 5 meters apart, the corner is a right angle.

questions.q: How long is the diagonal of Lucia's field?
questions.a: 50 meters

questions.q: Why is the diagonal the hypotenuse of the triangle?
questions.a: It is opposite the right angle at the corner, and it is the longest side of the triangle.

questions.q: Show that sides of 3, 4 and 5 meters make a right triangle.
questions.a: 3² + 4² = 9 + 16 = 25, and 5² = 25, so the sides satisfy the converse.

wdntb.why: The sets 3, 4, 5 and 5, 12, 13 and 6, 8, 10 are Pythagorean triples. For 4, 5, 6, the sum 16 + 25 = 41 does not equal 36.

noticeWonder.prompt: A square with sides of 3 units and a square with sides of 4 units sit on the two legs of a right triangle. A square with sides of 5 units sits on the hypotenuse. What do you notice about the areas 9, 16 and 25? What do you wonder?

asn.claim: The Pythagorean theorem works for every triangle.
asn.why: It only holds when the triangle has a right angle. In a triangle with sides 5, 6 and 8, the sum 25 + 36 is not 64.

asn.claim: In a right triangle, the hypotenuse is the longest side.
asn.why: The hypotenuse is opposite the largest angle, the right angle, and the longest side is always opposite the largest angle.

wyr.q: To find the distance between two points on a grid, would you rather draw a right triangle or use the distance formula?

compare.a: Uma finds the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs of 5 and 12 by computing 5² + 12² = 169 and then the square root, 13.
compare.b: Vic adds the legs, 5 + 12 = 17, and says the hypotenuse is 17.
compare.prompt: One strategy is flawed. Which one, and how can you check it using the squares of the sides?

debate.claim: A calculator makes it unnecessary to understand why the Pythagorean theorem works.
debate.forEvidence: A calculator gives the answer instantly once the right numbers are entered.
debate.againstEvidence: You still must decide which side is the hypotenuse and which sides are the legs, and that choice needs understanding.

listening.script: Listen to Ines find the distance between two points. The points are 1 comma 2 and 7 comma 10. She draws a right triangle with one horizontal leg and one vertical leg. The horizontal leg is 7 minus 1, which is 6 units. The vertical leg is 10 minus 2, which is 8 units. She squares each leg to get 36 and 64, and adds them to get 100. The distance is the square root of 100, which is 10 units. Ines says the distance is the hypotenuse, so it must be longer than either leg.

tasks.q: How long is the vertical leg?
tasks.why: The vertical leg goes from 2 to 10, and 10 − 2 = 8.

tasks.q: Why must the distance be longer than either leg?
options: It is the hypotenuse, the longest side of the right triangle.
It is found by adding the legs.
tasks.why: The hypotenuse is opposite the right angle, so it is longer than each leg.

story.title: The Banner Ladder
story.goal: choose a ladder long enough to reach the banner hook
story.intro: Diego must hang a banner on a hook high on the gym wall. He knows how high the hook is and how far from the wall the ladder can stand, so he needs to find the length of ladder that fits.

beats.lead: Diego draws a right triangle for the wall, the floor and the ladder.
beats.success: He labels the legs and the hypotenuse correctly, so the setup is clear.
beats.redirect: The labels look wrong, so Diego finds the right angle and starts over.

beats.lead: Diego uses the theorem to find the missing length.
beats.success: He squares, adds or subtracts correctly and takes the square root.
beats.redirect: His answer is longer than the legs added together, so he checks whether he forgot the square root.

beats.lead: Diego checks that the answer is reasonable for the real wall.
beats.success: The ladder is longer than the height of the hook, so the answer makes sense.
beats.redirect: The ladder length seems too short, so Diego checks which side is the hypotenuse.

story.ending: Diego picks a ladder with confidence and explains how the right triangle told him its length.

panels.says: A right triangle has legs of 6 and 8. I added the squares and got 100, so the hypotenuse is 100.
The two legs add up to only 14. Can one side be as long as 100?
Oh. The 100 is the square of the hypotenuse, not the side.
So what number times itself makes 100?

predict.q: Before Mateo answers, predict the length of the hypotenuse of the triangle with legs 6 and 8.
predict.why: The sum of the squares is 36 + 64 = 100, and the square root of 100 is 10.

transfer.relationship: The square of the longest side equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides in a right triangle
phrasings: a² + b² = c²
Legs of 30 and 40 give a hypotenuse of 50.
The diagonal of a 30 by 40 rectangle
The distance from (0, 0) to (30, 40)

decoys.why: This adds the lengths of the legs, but the hypotenuse is shorter than the two legs added together.
The sum of the squares is 2,500, so 50 is its square root, not the sum itself.

modeling.title: Choosing a ladder
modeling.scenario: A fictional school club needs to reach a banner hook that is 12 feet up a wall. The base of the ladder will stand 5 feet from the wall on level ground. The numbers are invented for this exercise.

given.label: Distance from the wall to the base

assumptions: The wall is straight up and the floor is level, so they meet at a right angle.
The ladder is a straight line that touches the hook exactly.
The measurements are accurate to the nearest foot.
prompts: Draw the right triangle and label the legs and the hypotenuse.
Find the length of the ladder that just reaches the hook.
A 15 foot ladder has its base 9 feet from the wall. How high up the wall does it reach?
limits: Real ladders must extend past the hook and follow safety rules the model leaves out.
The model treats the ladder as a line with no width.

sentence.base: The hypotenuse of the right triangle is 50 meters.
sentence.because: The hypotenuse is 50 meters because 30² + 40² = 2,500 and the square root of 2,500 is 50.
sentence.but: The diagonal is longer than each leg, but it is shorter than the two legs added together.
sentence.so: The marks are 3, 4 and 5 meters apart, so by the converse the corner is a right angle.

diagnostic.prompt: A right triangle has legs of 5 and 12. Find the hypotenuse. Then tell whether a triangle with sides 6, 7 and 10 is a right triangle.
lookFor: Finds 5² + 12² = 169 and a hypotenuse of 13
Tests 6² + 7² = 85 against 10² = 100 and says it is not a right triangle
Puts the longest side in the c position
diagnostic.language: Let the student draw and label the triangle with the right angle marked before computing. If the labels are right, the barrier is the vocabulary or explaining, not the calculation.

extension.task: Find two points on a coordinate grid that are exactly 13 units apart. Show your right triangle.
extension.reasoning: Explain why the distance formula is the Pythagorean theorem in disguise.

en.learning: Your child is learning that in a right triangle, the squares of the two shorter sides add up to the square of the longest side.
en.say: A right triangle has a square corner. The longest side is the one across from the corner.
en.ask: A ladder base is 3 feet from a wall and the ladder reaches 4 feet up. How long is the ladder?

es.learning: Su hijo o hija está aprendiendo que en un triángulo rectángulo, los cuadrados de los dos lados más cortos suman el cuadrado del lado más largo.

skills.languageObjective: I will describe an association using because, but and so with the words scatter plot, association and line of best fit.
successCriteria: I describe a scatter plot as positive, negative or no association, and as linear or not.
I spot clusters and outliers and say how they affect the pattern.
I use a given line of best fit to predict a value and say what the slope and y-intercept mean.
I explain why an association does not prove that one thing causes the other.

The slope means that for each extra ___, the predicted ___ changes by ___.

Argue why a pattern is not proof of a cause

vocab.def: A graph of points that shows how two measured quantities are related.
vocab.example: A graph with hours studied across the bottom and quiz score up the side
vocab.nonExample: A bar graph of the favorite colors in a class
vocab.sentence: Each point on the scatter plot is one student.

vocab.def: A pattern in how two quantities change together.
vocab.example: As hours studied go up, quiz scores tend to go up
vocab.nonExample: A claim that studying causes every score
vocab.sentence: The scatter plot shows a positive association.
vocab.everyday: A club or group of people with a shared goal
vocab.morphology: as- means toward and socius means companion

vocab.def: A data point that is far away from the pattern of the other points.
vocab.example: A 4 centimeter plant when similar plants are about 15 centimeters
vocab.nonExample: A point that sits right on the trend
vocab.sentence: The outlier is far below the line.
vocab.morphology: out and lie, a point that lies outside the pattern

vocab.def: A straight line drawn close to the points to show the overall trend.
vocab.example: y = 6x + 50 for the study-time points
vocab.nonExample: A line that connects every point in order
vocab.sentence: The line of best fit lets us predict a quiz score.

vocab.def: A group of data points that are close together.
vocab.example: Five points that sit near the same part of the line
vocab.nonExample: One point far from the others
vocab.sentence: The points form a cluster near the line.
vocab.everyday: A bunch of things growing or gathered closely together, like grapes

vocab.def: A table that shows counts for two categories at the same time.
vocab.example: A table with grade level in the rows and lunch choice in the columns
vocab.nonExample: A table with one list of names
vocab.sentence: A two-way table shows how many students fit each pair of categories.

misconceptions.belief: If two quantities have an association, one of them causes the other.
misconceptions.why: A clear pattern feels like an explanation, and everyday speech links together with because.
misconceptions.fix: Ask what else could change both quantities. List at least one other factor before claiming a cause.

errorCase.story: Tara studies a scatter plot of shoe size and reading score for students in grades 1 to 8.
steps: The points rise from left to right, so the association is positive.
So having bigger feet causes a student to read better.
errorCase.explain: Older students tend to have bigger feet and also more reading practice. Age affects both, so the association does not show that one causes the other.

misconceptions.belief: The slope of a line of best fit is the predicted value when x is 0.
misconceptions.why: Students mix up the number multiplied by x with the number added at the end of the equation.
misconceptions.fix: Test x = 0 and x = 1 in the equation. The first output is the starting value, and the jump to the second is the slope.

errorCase.story: Dev reads the line y = 6x + 50, where x is hours studied and y is the predicted quiz score.
steps: The line is y = 6x + 50, and the slope is 6.
So a student who studies 0 hours is predicted to score 6.
Studying 1 hour adds 50 points.
errorCase.explain: The slope 6 means each extra hour goes with about 6 more points. The y-intercept 50 is the predicted score for 0 hours.

misconceptions.belief: A line of best fit can predict values anywhere, even far outside the data.
misconceptions.why: A line goes on forever on the graph, so students trust it forever, even where the data stop.
misconceptions.fix: Mark the range of the data. Predictions inside it are reasonable. Outside it, check whether the answer is even possible.

errorCase.story: Omar uses the line y = 6x + 50 to predict a quiz score for a student who studies 10 hours. The data shows 1 to 7 hours.
steps: Put x = 10 into the line y = 6x + 50.
So the student will score 110 on a test that is out of 100.
errorCase.explain: A score of 110 is impossible on a test out of 100, and 10 hours is outside the data, which stopped at 7 hours. The line is only a good guide near the data.

misconceptions.belief: Best fit means the line must go through every point.
misconceptions.why: In everyday speech, a thing that fits best fits exactly, so students expect the line to touch every point.
misconceptions.fix: Compare to a coat that fits best overall. A line of best fit is the closest line to all points together, and some points are above or below it.

reading.title: Study Time and Quiz Scores
reading.text: Mina's class collects data on hours studied and quiz scores for 7 students and makes a scatter plot. The points rise from left to right, so there is a positive association. The class draws a line of best fit with the equation y = 6x + 50, where x is hours studied and y is the predicted score. The slope is 6, so each extra hour of study goes with about 6 more points. The y-intercept is 50, the predicted score for 0 hours. One student studied 7 hours and scored 93, close to the predicted 92. The points form a cluster near the line, with no outlier. Mina warns that the line should not predict a score for 10 hours, because 6 × 10 + 50 = 110 is more than the highest possible score of 100.
reading.simple: Mina's class collects data on hours studied and quiz scores for 7 students. The scatter plot rises from left to right, so there is a positive association. The line of best fit is y = 6x + 50. The slope is 6, so each extra hour goes with about 6 more points. The y-intercept is 50, the score predicted for 0 hours. One student studied 7 hours and scored 93, close to the predicted 92. Do not use the line for 10 hours, because it gives 110 and the highest score is 100.

questions.q: What is the equation of the line of best fit?
Why should Mina not use the line to predict the score for 10 hours?
questions.a: 10 hours is outside the data, and the line gives 110, which is more than the highest possible score of 100.

questions.q: Use the line to predict the score for 4 hours of study.

items: Temperature and sales of cold drinks
Hours of practice and number of goals
Age of a phone and its price
wdntb.why: The first three pairs have a positive association, because both quantities tend to increase together. The age of a phone and its price have a negative association.

noticeWonder.prompt: A scatter plot has eight points that rise from left to right and one point far below the others. What do you notice about the pattern? What do you wonder about the point that is far away?

asn.claim: A positive association means that one quantity causes the other to increase.
asn.why: An association only shows that the quantities change together. A third factor, like hot weather, can change both.

asn.claim: A scatter plot with a negative association has a line of best fit with a negative slope.
asn.why: A negative association means y tends to decrease as x increases, so the line falls from left to right and its slope is negative.

wyr.q: Would you rather describe a scatter plot with words like positive and negative, or with the equation of a line of best fit?

compare.a: Ana uses the line y = 6x + 50 to predict the score for 4 hours: 6 × 4 + 50 = 74.
compare.b: Ben reads the score for 4 hours straight from the nearest point on the plot, which is 75.
compare.prompt: Both numbers are close. Which one is a prediction from the line, and which is an actual data value?

debate.claim: A line of best fit should be used to predict values far outside the data.
debate.forEvidence: A line is a steady pattern, so continuing it gives a reasonable guess for any x.
debate.againstEvidence: Patterns can change outside the data. The line predicts 110 for 10 hours, which is impossible on a test with a top score of 100.

listening.script: Listen to Jorge describe a scatter plot of bean plants. Each point is one plant. The horizontal axis shows the days since planting, and the vertical axis shows the height in centimeters. The points rise from left to right, so the association is positive. The line of best fit is y equals 2x plus 3. The slope is 2, so the plants grew about 2 centimeters each day. At 10 days the line predicts 23 centimeters. One plant, at 6 days, is only 4 centimeters tall. That point is far below the line, so Jorge calls it an outlier.

tasks.q: What height does the line predict at 10 days?
tasks.why: Putting x = 10 into y = 2x + 3 gives 2 × 10 + 3 = 23.

tasks.q: Why does Jorge call the 4 centimeter plant an outlier?
options: It is far from the pattern of the other points.
tasks.why: At 6 days the line predicts 15 centimeters, so a plant at 4 centimeters is far below the pattern.

story.title: Practice Makes a Pattern
story.goal: find out whether more practice goes with more goals
story.intro: Omar keeps the team records for the school soccer club. He has the weekly practice hours and the goals for each player, and the coach asks him to show whether there is a pattern.

beats.lead: Omar plots each player as a point, with practice hours on the horizontal axis and goals on the vertical axis.
beats.success: The points show a clear direction, so Omar describes the association in a full sentence.
beats.redirect: The axes are mixed up, so Omar checks which quantity belongs on each axis.

beats.lead: Omar uses the coach's line of best fit to predict the goals for a player who practices 5 hours.
beats.success: The prediction is near the data, so Omar explains what the slope means.
beats.redirect: The prediction looks too high, so Omar checks whether it is inside the range of the data.

beats.lead: Omar writes a note for the coach about what the pattern does and does not show.
beats.success: He says the pattern is an association and names another factor that might matter.
beats.redirect: His note says practice causes goals, so Omar rewrites it to describe an association only.

story.ending: The coach reads Omar's note and uses the pattern to plan practice, knowing it is a guide and not a proof.

panels.says: Ice cream sales and sunburns both go up in the summer, so ice cream causes sunburns.
The scatter plot shows a positive association.
So one must cause the other.
What else changes in the summer?
Hot, sunny weather! It affects both. An association is a pattern, not a cause.

predict.q: Before Luis changes his claim, predict the best explanation for the positive association between ice cream sales and sunburns.
options: Sunburns make people buy ice cream
predict.why: Sunny weather leads to more ice cream sales and to more sunburns, so a third factor explains the pattern.

transfer.relationship: As one quantity increases, the other tends to increase by about the same amount each time
phrasings: The points rise from left to right and lie near the line y = 6x + 50.
There is a positive association between hours studied and quiz score.
A table: 1, 2 and 3 hours match about 56, 62 and 68 points.
Each extra hour of study goes with about 6 more points.

decoys.why: This claims a cause and an exact amount, but the line shows only a trend and the points do not all sit on it.

modeling.title: Practice hours and goals

Practice hours are the number of hours per week for the whole season.
The line is a summary of the trend and not an exact rule.

Say what the slope and the y-intercept mean in this situation.
Predict the goals for a player who practices 5 hours, and explain why predicting for 20 hours is not a good idea.

Practice hours are only one factor, and the data do not show that practice causes goals.

sentence.base: The scatter plot shows a positive association.
sentence.because: The scatter plot shows a positive association because the points rise from left to right near the line of best fit.
sentence.but: The points do not all lie on the line of best fit, but the association is still clear.

en.learning: Your child is learning to read graphs of paired data to see whether two things tend to go up together, go in opposite directions or show no pattern.

en.ask: On hot days more people buy cold drinks. Does buying cold drinks make the day hot? Why or why not?

vocab.morphology: ad- means toward and sumere means to take, so assume means take on as true

vocab.def: The output of a linear model when the input is 0, where the graph starts.
vocab.example: The 150 dollar fee in C = 6n + 150
vocab.nonExample: The 6 dollars, which is charged for each student
vocab.sentence: The initial value is the cost before any students ride.

vocab.def: A claim supported by evidence and reasoning that others can check.
vocab.example: Company A is cheaper for 38 or more students, because 6n + 150 is less than 10n then
vocab.nonExample: Company A is better because I like it

misconceptions.belief: A model gives the exact answer for the real world.
misconceptions.why: Students trust a computed number because the arithmetic is exact, and forget that the situation was simplified.
misconceptions.fix: Say predicts instead of is. Name what the model leaves out before you state the number.

errorCase.story: Tia uses the model C = 6n + 150 for a bus trip with 45 students.
steps: The model is C = 6n + 150.
So the trip will cost exactly 420 dollars, with nothing else to pay.
errorCase.explain: The number 420 is the model's prediction if its assumptions hold. A tip for the driver or a toll is not in the model, so the real cost could be higher.

misconceptions.belief: The first number in the description always goes with the variable.
misconceptions.why: Students write the numbers in the order they read them and do not check which one repeats.
misconceptions.fix: Ask which amount is paid once and which amount is paid for each person. The repeated amount multiplies the variable.

errorCase.story: Kai writes a model for Company A, which charges a fee of 150 dollars and 6 dollars for each student.
steps: Company A charges a fee of 150 dollars and 6 dollars per student.
The first number I read goes with n, so C = 150n + 6.
For 10 students, C = 150 × 10 + 6 = 1,506 dollars.
errorCase.explain: The 6 dollars repeats for each student, so it multiplies n, and the 150 dollar fee is paid once: C = 6n + 150. For 10 students, the cost is 6 × 10 + 150 = 210 dollars.

misconceptions.belief: The option with the lower rate is always the better choice.
misconceptions.why: Students compare only the number that repeats and overlook the starting amount that sets where the lines begin.
misconceptions.fix: Compare the totals for a small group and for a large group. The better option can change, so find where the two models are equal.

errorCase.story: Mia compares Company A, C = 6n + 150, with Company B, C = 10n.
steps: Company A charges 6 dollars per student and Company B charges 10 dollars per student.
Since 6 is less than 10, Company A is cheaper for every group.
So the club should always choose Company A.
errorCase.explain: The 150 dollar fee matters for small groups. For 20 students, A costs 6 × 20 + 150 = 270 dollars and B costs 10 × 20 = 200 dollars. A is cheaper only from 38 students on.

misconceptions.belief: An assumption is something we know is true.
misconceptions.why: In everyday speech, people assume things without checking, and some students hear the word as sure or as careless.
misconceptions.fix: Say in class that an assumption is a choice we state out loud so others can test it, and write the sentence frame We assume that ___.

reading.title: Choosing a Bus
reading.text: A school club plans a trip to the science museum. Company A charges a 150 dollar fee plus 6 dollars for each student. Company B charges 10 dollars for each student and no fee. Zara builds a linear model for each company, where n is the number of students and C is the cost. Her models are C = 6n + 150 and C = 10n. She states an assumption: the prices stay the same all day. She sets the models equal and gets n = 37.5. Her argument is that Company A is cheaper for 38 or more students. For 40 students, Company A costs 390 dollars and Company B costs 400 dollars. She also names a limitation: the model ignores the bus limit of 50 students.
reading.simple: A club plans a trip to a museum. Company A charges a 150 dollar fee and 6 dollars for each student. Company B charges 10 dollars for each student. Zara builds a model for each company: C = 6n + 150 and C = 10n. She assumes the prices stay the same. The models are equal at n = 37.5. So Company A is cheaper for 38 or more students. For 40 students, A costs 390 dollars and B costs 400 dollars. A limitation is the bus limit of 50 students.

questions.q: What is Zara's model for Company B?
questions.a: C = 10n

questions.q: Why does Zara say Company A is cheaper for 38 or more students and not for 37.5?
questions.a: A group cannot have half a student. At 37 students B costs 370 and A costs 372, but at 38 students A costs 378 and B costs 380.

questions.q: Check that Company A costs less than Company B for 40 students.
questions.a: A: 6 × 40 + 150 = 390. B: 10 × 40 = 400. Since 390 is less than 400, A costs less.

items: Assumption: the prices stay the same
wdntb.why: The rate, the initial value and the assumption are choices that build the model. The prediction is a result computed from the model.

noticeWonder.prompt: Company A is C = 6n + 150 and Company B is C = 10n. For 20 students, A costs 270 dollars and B costs 200 dollars. For 40 students, A costs 390 dollars and B costs 400 dollars. What do you notice? What do you wonder?

asn.claim: A mathematical model is useful only if it matches reality exactly.
asn.why: Every model simplifies. A model is useful when its assumptions are stated and its predictions are close enough to help a decision.

asn.claim: Changing an assumption can change the conclusion of a model.
asn.why: The conclusion comes from the model, and the model comes from its assumptions, so a different assumption can lead to a different result.

wyr.q: To argue for a choice, would you rather show a graph of both models or a table of costs?

compare.a: Zara sets 6n + 150 = 10n, solves n = 37.5 and says Company A is cheaper from 38 students.
compare.b: Tomas tests 36, 37, 38 and 39 students in a table and sees the cheaper company switch between 37 and 38.
compare.prompt: Both reach the same conclusion. How do the two approaches support each other?

debate.claim: A model that ignores the driver's tip is not a good model.
debate.forEvidence: The real cost will be higher than the prediction, so a club could plan its money badly.
debate.againstEvidence: Every model leaves something out. If the tip is small and the same for both companies, it does not change which company is cheaper.

listening.script: Listen to Tariq present a model. A tutoring club charges 8 dollars for each session plus a 12 dollar sign-up fee. Tariq writes T equals 8s plus 12, where s is the number of sessions. For 5 sessions, the model predicts 52 dollars. Tariq states his assumption: the price per session does not change. He also names a limit: the model only works up to 20 sessions, because that is all the club offers. Then he makes an argument. If a family has 60 dollars, they can afford 6 sessions, because 8 times 6 plus 12 is 60.

tasks.q: What does the model predict for 5 sessions?
tasks.why: Putting s = 5 into T = 8s + 12 gives 8 × 5 + 12 = 52.

tasks.q: Which statement is Tariq's assumption?
options: The price per session does not change.
tasks.why: He chooses to treat the price as steady. The 20 sessions is a limit, and the 60 dollars is a condition of the family.

story.title: The Can Drive Plan
story.goal: decide how many cans to collect to pay for a new club banner
story.intro: Rosa's club wants a new banner, and the recycling center pays by the can. She must build a model for the money, choose a plan and be ready to defend it to the club.

beats.lead: Rosa writes a linear model for the money earned, using the amount per can and any starting amount.
beats.success: Each number in the model matches a fact, so she can say what it means.
beats.redirect: One number is in the wrong place, so Rosa asks which amount repeats for every can.

beats.lead: Rosa uses the model to predict how many cans the club needs.
beats.success: She checks that the number makes sense for the school and states her assumptions.
beats.redirect: The prediction is too large to be reasonable, so she checks whether the model still fits that many cans.

beats.lead: A club member challenges Rosa's assumption that the center will keep paying the same price.
beats.success: Rosa tests a lower price, shows how the plan changes and revises her recommendation.
beats.redirect: Rosa ignores the challenge at first, then sees that an assumption that might fail must be named.

story.ending: The club agrees on a plan, and Rosa's argument shows the model, the evidence and the limits.

panels.says: My model says the museum trip will cost exactly 420 dollars.
What did you assume?
That the prices never change and there are no other costs.
What if the driver needs a tip?
Then the cost goes up. I should say about 420 dollars and list my assumptions.

predict.q: Before Eli rewrites his claim, predict the best way to state the model's result.
options: The model predicts about 420 dollars if the prices stay the same and there are no extra costs.
The model is wrong because it cannot be exact.
predict.why: A good statement gives the prediction and the assumptions behind it. A model does not need to be exact to be useful.

A line that starts at (0, 150) and rises 6 for each student
A table: 0, 10 and 20 students cost 150, 210 and 270 dollars

decoys.why: The cost rises by 60 and then by 90, so the rate of change is not constant and the model is not linear.

modeling.title: Choosing a sound system
modeling.scenario: A fictional school radio club can rent a sound system from two shops. Shop A charges 40 dollars to set up plus 15 dollars for each hour. Shop B charges 100 dollars to set up plus 5 dollars for each hour. The prices are invented for this exercise.
assumptions: Each shop charges its set-up fee once and its hourly price for each whole hour.
The prices stay the same for the whole event.
The two sound systems work equally well for the club.
prompts: Write a linear model for each shop and say what each number means.
Argue which shop the club should choose for a 4 hour event and for an 8 hour event, using evidence from the models.
State two assumptions and one limitation of your argument.
limits: The models leave out delivery costs, damage fees and any discount the shops might give.
The club may not know the length of the event, so the best choice could change.

sentence.base: The linear model C = 6n + 150 predicts the cost of the trip.
sentence.because: The model predicts 420 dollars for 45 students because 6 × 45 + 150 = 420.
sentence.but: The model predicts the cost well, but it leaves out extra costs like a tip for the driver.
sentence.so: The prices might change, so the club should state its assumption before it trusts the prediction.

diagnostic.prompt: A gym charges a 30 dollar sign-up fee and 20 dollars per month. Write a linear model, predict the cost for 6 months, and state one assumption and one limitation.
lookFor: Writes C = 20m + 30 with the rate and the initial value in the right places
Predicts 150 dollars for 6 months
States an assumption, such as a steady price, and a limitation, such as no cancellation fees
diagnostic.language: Let the student say the model aloud with the words fee once and price each month before writing. If the model is correct, the barrier is the vocabulary of argument, not the mathematics.

extension.task: Choose a real decision you face, such as two bus passes or two data plans. Build a linear model for each option, find where they cost the same and write a short argument for which one to choose.
extension.reasoning: Explain what would change in your argument if one of your assumptions were false.

en.learning: Your child is learning to build a simple math rule for a real situation, use it to predict, and explain what it leaves out.
en.say: A model is a simple picture of real life. A good thinker says what the model assumes and where it might be wrong.
en.ask: A taxi costs 3 dollars to start and 2 dollars for each mile. What would a 10 mile ride cost, and what might make the real price different?
en.activity: Look at a store flyer with a membership deal, like a card with a yearly fee. Ask your child to write a rule for the total cost with and without the card and decide when the card is worth it.

es.learning: Su hijo o hija está aprendiendo a crear una regla matemática sencilla para una situación real, a usarla para hacer predicciones y a explicar qué deja fuera.
es.say: Un modelo es una imagen sencilla de la vida real. Quien piensa bien dice qué supone su modelo y en qué podría fallar.
es.ask: Un taxi cobra 3 dólares al empezar y 2 dólares por cada milla. ¿Cuánto costaría un viaje de 10 millas y qué podría hacer que el precio real sea distinto?
es.activity: Miren un folleto de una tienda con una oferta de membresía, como una tarjeta con una cuota anual. Pidan a su hijo o hija que escriba una regla para el costo total con la tarjeta y sin ella, y que decida cuándo vale la pena.
